sentences.text: There is one rule and it is the only thing about the whole business that anybody argues over.
The name cannot be your own.
There is a second rule that is not really a rule, which is that you do not tell anybody afterwards whose name you said.
Nobody enforces that one either.

It gets broken constantly by children and almost never by anybody over about twenty, and Xuan has never worked out at what point in a person's life it stops being a game and starts being the sort of thing you keep.
That is absolute and it is enforced by nothing at all, which Xuan found remarkable when he first understood it.
Nobody can hear what you say.

You are twenty metres out in a noisy river with your back to the bank and there are fifty people talking behind you, and if you said your own name every year of your life not one person would ever know.
He asked his father about this at about ten, in the way children ask a question they think is clever.

His father said: "And?" "So how do you know nobody does?" "I don't." "So the rule doesn't do anything." His father was mending a net, which is when the useful conversations happened in that house, and he did not look up.
"It does everything," he said.
"It's the only part of it that does anything at all.
You stand in a cold river in June and you have got about four minutes to pick one person out of everybody you have ever known, and it can't be you." He pulled a knot.
"That's the whole event, Xuan.

Everything else is queueing." Xuan thought about that for a year and came back at eleven with what he considered to be a serious objection, which was that most people obviously just said their mother.
"Most people do," his father agreed.

"The first six or seven times." "So it's still nothing." "Ask your uncle Nel who he said in 1994." Xuan did, eventually, about four years later, and got an answer that took him completely by surprise and that is not his to write down.
Xuan asked what happened to the name.
"It goes upriver." He said it the way you would say that a road goes to Oviedo.
"And then?" "And then nothing.
It gets to the top and that's the end of it.
There's no more to it than that and anybody who tells you different is selling something." Xuan said, with some heat, that in that case the whole thing was pointless.
He was ten and he had been building to this for the whole conversation and he delivered it with a certain amount of triumph.
And his father put the net down for the first time in the conversation and said: "Yes.
That's right.
And the whole village turns out for it every June and has done since before anybody can tell you, so you might want to have another think about what *pointless* means."
